correctness.rationale: Six explicit unimodular matrices arise from the exact normalization; the two parity-preserving digit maps generate upper and even-lower elementary transvections. Explicit constructions cover odd-second-coordinate vectors at powers of two; elementary elimination covers primitive pairs at odd prime powers, and CRT gives all moduli. Digit one maps the parity branches bijectively. All transitions are permutations on the orbit, and irreducible/aperiodic finite-state mixing proves limiting densities. Exact marginal counts, valuation differences, CRT independence, and a 4-state matrix with eigenvalues 3,-1,1,1 prove each asserted formula. Independent original-ring recurrence and orbit tests passed; they are supplementary only.

originality.rationale: The normalized ternary sequence is the algebraic-integer object of Northshield and Spiegelhofer. Their inspected recurrence, symmetry and rational-enumeration statements do not give a uniform modular primitive-pair orbit, the three-to-one dyadic bias, independence of all finite sets of valuations, or the exact ternary-block parity count. The closest modular Stern records concern different binary or polynomial recurrences; general group and random-walk methods are not claimed as novel. Specific same-object and generalization searches found no equivalent. Unindexed literature remains a risk.
residual_risks: Unindexed or differently titled equivalent modular laws for the normalized ternary sequence may exist.
Related modular equidistribution records for other Stern-type objects were seen at summary level only; those summaries cannot certify full-text noncoverage.
The claim uses standard finite-state and modular-group tools and claims novelty only for their precise application and resulting complete laws.

value.rationale: The object is a canonical ternary rational-enumerating algebraic-integer analogue of Stern, naturally normalized into integers. Its modular-frequency invariant was not specified by the motivating reversal and enumeration results. The complete all-modulus distribution exposes the nontrivial 3:1 dyadic bias, independent odd-prime and dyadic valuation laws, and an exact every-level parity census; the classification gives usable local statistics for arbitrarily many moduli without arbitrary parameter slicing.
